title: House Health & Human Services [Aug 22, 2025 - Upon Adjournment]

utterances.text: The House Health and Human Services Committee will come to order. Mr. Shadun, please call the roll. Representative Bradfield. Here. Yeah. English. Excused. Here. Gilchrist. Excused. Here. Here. Johnson. Here. Ryden. Here. Stewart K. Here. Stewart R. Here. Leader. Here. Mr. Chair. Here. We have the entire House of Stewart in the House today. Welcome to Health and Human Services. We will hear two bills today in our committee. We will start with Senate Bill 2, and then we will move to Senate Bill 3

. It looks like we have bill sponsors here with us. Uh, who would like to begin? Representative Wilford. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair and members of the committee, for taking time to consider Senate Bill 2 this special session. I'm really proud to be bringing this bill along with my co-prime assistant Majority Leader Bacon. As we're discussing an array of topics and making really difficult decisions in such a short amount of time, I want to provide a little bit of background and statistics for

you for a bit of context as to why we're having this conversation and why this bill in particular is so important to pass. On July 4th, with the passage of H.R. 1, Planned Parenthood was immediately removed from the federal Medicaid program. This made it completely impossible for Planned Parenthood of the Rocky Mountains to see Medicaid patients, which meant that they had to very quickly cancel appointments that were scheduled for the very next day. On July 7th, Planned Parenthood filed an emer

gency motion, and a judge issued a temporary restraining order, which was amended on July 11th. However, this was— this didn't happen before 991 patient appointments had been canceled and before Planned Parenthood was able to restore services under the temporary restraining order on July 16th. This was then followed by additional canceled appointments after the temporary restraining order expired and before it was replaced by an injunction, which the federal government has appealed and which cou

ld be stayed by the Supreme Court any day now. This was a significant disruption in critical care and timely support for patients and a significant moral injury for the providers who were were provided— prevented and prohibited from serving them. Colorado Medicaid patients cannot see non-Medicaid providers for covered services. So while generally beneficial, this, this prevents Medicaid patients from self-paying at Planned Parenthood so long as Planned Parenthood is a part of Medicaid. So some a

dditional facts about Planned Parenthood for your consideration: Planned Parenthood is an essential, irreplaceable piece of Colorado's primary and reproductive healthcare system and healthcare safety net. They provide over 55 visits annually. 1 in 3 women nationally receive care at Planned Parenthood, including 45% of Black women, 43% of Medicaid enrollees, and 21% of Republican women receive care at Planned Parenthood. Furthermore, a study found that 88% of Democrats and 64% of Republicans oppo

se Congress or the Trump administration taking away funds from Planned Parenthood. 77% of all voters oppose Congress or the Trump administration taking away funds from Planned Parenthood, and 57% of voters who want abortion to be illegal oppose Congress or the Trump administration taking away funds from Planned Parenthood. And these numbers really do go to demonstrate that access to Planned Parenthood, which provides a range of essential care, isn't and should not be a partisan issue, but should

be one fundamentally about access to healthcare. Care. So when we're thinking about what needs to be done, there is a need to restore access to over 11,000 Coloradans so that they can continue to be seen at Planned Parenthood by authorizing HCPOF to use state funds to pay for claims to federally prohibited entities in the absence of a federal match. And I'm going to turn it over to my co-prime to speak more about that specific fix that we're offering in this bill. Thank you, Representative— uh,

sorry, Assistant Majority Leader Bacon. Thank you for joining us. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you to my co-prime. And so, as you can see, the bill is very short and straightforward, but what it does— Section 71113 prohibits federal Medicaid payment to nonprofit healthcare providers if the provider does 3 things. First, primarily provides family planning services reproductive health services and related care. Second, offers abortions outside of the limited Hyde exceptions. And third, receive

d federal and state Medicaid payments totaling more than $800,000 in fiscal year 2023. The bill provides state-only funding through our, uh, uh, HCPOF, if you will, to prohibited entities as defined in that section of H.R. 1 so long as the prohibition is in effect, as you heard from my co-prime in reference to the injunction. And so while an entity is eligible to receive federal reimbursements from CMS, like PPRM or Planned Parenthood Rocky Mountains currently is during the injunction, there is

no need for state-only payments because there is still a federal match. This language is carefully crafted to stabilize the federal roller coaster, and with the department's support, it gives HCPOF the authority to ensure the continuity of care. And so in closing, um, we just wanted to note again why we are bringing this bill forward before we go to questions in the witness phase. As you heard from our co-prime, you heard the statistics, but more importantly, we want to go back to the number of

people whose healthcare will be impacted, quite frankly, by the provisions of H.R. 1. Not only are we trying to figure out how to support thousands of people that may not be able to be absorbed into you other, know, systems of care, let alone to be able to provide providers. But there are a lot of places and corners of the state in which the providers, as described by HR1, and in our case it just happens to be one type of provider, that provider is the only provider in the area. And so if we do

not figure out how to support this entity, that means there are whole communities that will not have health care. I don't— I also want to say this is not political to the extent that people want to make it. I know what I just said is true, that the entity that is impacted by this provision of H.R. 1 is truly the healthcare provider for whole communities. It is true because it was true for me. I also want to recognize that one of the flagship entities in City and County of Denver is in my distric

t. When I first moved to Colorado, Planned Parenthood of the Rocky Mountains was my healthcare provider. And people go there for so many other things. I went there for, you know, blood pressure medicine, which we all know, me working in this building, requires. And so I just want to have us keep that in mind This is real life. I hope that we can move beyond politics to recognize something that has been important to us here in this building for a very long time. You know, Colorado has committed t

o, quite frankly, trying to figure out how to cover all Coloradans. And when we think about what it takes and what we're looking for with this funding, uh, that's what we intend to do. And so also, as you look at a potential fiscal note. And again, if the injunction stays in place, we will not need to look to it. But if it doesn't, just— we just want to be able to remind you all that we have existing funds and existing structures that we are currently paying to be able to cover all Coloradans, e

ven in certain exceptions that we're doing now, particularly with, you know, the federal government's already current programming and current position on coverage of abortions, for example, we have already taken positions and steps to be able to cover certain practices as well as certain circumstances to be sure that people have health care. And so we believe that the funding that we're providing here would extend the idea to reimbursing providers that are excluded. And so relative to that conce

pt, you know, $4.3 as compared to the $17 billion budget that is HCPOF. When we think about some of those places where PPRM is the exclusive healthcare provider, it is a very, very small percentage that has actually already been budgeted for. If you think about projections versus actuals, that is already within the concepts and constructs that we have prepared for to be able to cover people who may need to be covered outside of already current programs. And so therefore, we believe these costs a

re absorbable within the program and therefore not an excessive burden at all. And so with that, we will pause. Again, thank you so much for your consideration today. We are very proud to bring it forward. We know this will do a great service to our neighbors. And with that, We'll stop for questions. Thank you, bill sponsors. Appreciate that. do have a question on what process will HCPUF use to identify entities that are prohibited from receiving federal reimbursement? And how will this information be verified? Go ahead. Sorry. Sorry. Rep. Wilford, go ahead. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, and thank you very much, Representative, for the question. So under HR 1, they're very specific about which providers are considered banned providers, and I'll be really explicit in that when we look at the healthcare landscape in Colora

do, the only provider that is considered a banned provider is Planned Parenthood. ments totaling more than $800,000 in FY 2020 2023 were banned. ave ideas, I can say we would probably be open to to that, but state-only Medicaid dollars felt like the best use of funds given that these are services specifically for Medicaid patients. on would not be reimbursed as a covered service. There is a separate fund for that. All right, what, what other questions do we have? All right, seeing none, let's move on to witness testimony. Thank you very much. Um, would you all prefer to have the proponents or the opponents come first? Let's have the opponents come first and then allow the proponents to round it out. Sounds great. All right, so, uh, I'd like to call up the following people: Scott Chamblin, Dr. Thomas Perrell, Nathan Fisher,

ome up as well, you're welcome to. I think we've filled out our panel. So, okay, let's go ahead. Mr. Chamblain, welcome back. You'll have 2 minutes to testify, and please introduce yourself. Thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. My name is Scott Chamblain. I'm the executive director of Colorado Right to Life, and we oppose this bill. I'd first apologize, skipping that part. n disqualified from receiving federal Medicaid dollars due to their involvement in what the bill euphemistically calls certain reproductive healthcare services. This bill, by the force of a gun, takes taxpayer dollars to financially sustain abortion providers like Planned Parenthood that have been deemed ineligible for federal funding because of their participation or association with the intentional killing of preborn children. This bill bypasses federal protections for life and forces Colorado

taxpayers, many of whom believe deeply in the sanctity of human life to subsidize organizations that end it. r. You don't need to recreate a wheel or go into hopeless abstraction. You only care about decisions that matter. When those decisions matter, the obligations don't need to be showstopping or onerous. Basic transparency. I think it's fair that citizens of their states should just understand what systems their gove

rnment is using in what situations, right? Agencies should conduct basic assessments. Just make sure the system is working as intended., right? Make sure half a million low-income people aren't going to get denied SNAP benefits because there's a bug in the code, right? This doesn't need to be PhD-level statistical testing. In many cases, it just needs to be basic quality assurance, right? And the final thing is basic explanations. This is not too much to ask if you're using a system that is prop

erly suited for the task at hand. Okay, think about like a FICO score. A credit score. If you have a low FICO score, FICO will tell you, well, your accounts are too new, or your balances are too high, or you have a recent late payment. Those are good explanations. They help explain why this score that's affecting your life came back, right? Public benefits eligibility systems should tell you, you don't meet this threshold. You have too much income, right? Like, we've assessed your needs in these

ways, and therefore, you've qualified for a lower set of services. That's not too much to ask. Employment evaluation systems, there should be metrics, right? There should be some metrics that people can understand as to why they lost their job or didn't get promoted. So I want to close by saying we've been dealing with automated decision systems for a long, long time. This stuff is not new. It's been challenging for a long, long time. The fact that we live in an LLM world now is, is really gas

on the fire. And this is a great, great time to step up as state legislators and remind government that they have these basic obligations to their citizens. That doesn't mean you have to throw all the technology out. That doesn't mean you have to have complex requirements that no one understands. Basic transparency, basic explanations, and basic due diligence could really go a long way here. And with that, I will wrap up and thank you very much for your time. Thank you very much. Appreciate the,

uh, the insights and, and for that analysis, especially from the, uh, the legal aspect and what's at stake. And, uh, Senator Marchman has a question. Thanks. And I've been pretty tangential to a lot of the AI conversations that have been having— that have been taking place, but one of the things I keep hearing is, and I even heard Today, we need a good definition of consequential decisions. If I'm not mistaken, what you're talking about related to that procedural due process and what the intent

ion, I think, was, was to make sure that a notice does happen if that AI was used in a consequential decision. Is it fair to say— again, not a lawyer, never got that degree— Is it fair to say that we could instruct organizations to look at things that would fall under that procedural due process as the list, so to speak, of what could be a consequential decision and therefore subject to the regulations that we put in place here in Colorado? That's a great question. Thank you, Senator. If you're

talking about private organizations, my personal opinion is it would be kind of awkward to lift the procedural due process, life, liberty, property, and put it on private companies just because that's obligations for government, right? I do think for government use that might work well. When I was brainstorming at the Federal Trade Commission about some similar sets of regulations for private entities, one approach we considered is just enumerate the major federal civil rights statutes, right? T

he Equal Credit Opportunity Act covers credit. Title VII covers employment. You can put together about half a dozen major civil rights statutes that date back to the '70s that really draw big circles around big consequential areas of life. And so that's another way that you could do consequential decisions. But I do agree that giving people notice when, whether that's government or private sector, you should know when you're in that bucket. But I think there's lots of clear ways to draw that lin

e, right? And I think that there's, you should not need to throw up your hands or get too theoretical to get that job done. Senator Marshall. Thank you. I should have known public versus private, but I really like what you said about, about all of it, but the civil rights states statutes in particular being, um, a good guide. So thank you. Thank you, Senator. All right, uh, any other questions from anybody else? We really appreciate you being here and being patient for the whole presentation. Th

ank you very much. Uh, all right, uh, Ms. Boggan, you are last but not Yes, thanks, Madam Chair and members of the committee for also being patient through all of these presentations. I'm sure there is a lot to chew on following this and so much to build on. I will similarly try to keep it concise and build on where Aaron left off, which is what are some actionable steps that can be taken or can be provided in guidance by legislators for government use of AI. So, uh, my name is Miranda Bogan. I'

m the director of the AI Governance Lab at the Center for Democracy and Technology, which is the leading nonpartisan nonprofit organization fighting to advance civil rights and civil liberties in the digital age. And my program there works on developing and promoting the adoption of robust, technically informed solutions for effective regulation and governance of AI systems. And I also bring a number of years of experience from the private sector advancing responsible AI and AI governance in lar

ge-scale enterprises. So I've been in, I've been in the shoes of the folks that you're trying to work with. So first, I'll say you're in great company as you're thinking about public sector use and guidance for that. According to my colleague's analysis, in 2025 alone, 50 bills were introduced across 20 states, with 14 passed into law, primarily focused on establishing safeguards for public sector AI use largely on matters including risk assessment, governance processes, and transparency. And ma

ny of those efforts mirror efforts at the federal level. The OMB guidance across two different administrations is relatively consistent. We're seeing a lot of the same priorities pop up in these state-level and sometimes local-level efforts. Things like risk management and transparency, central ownership like chief AI officers, interdisciplinary governance bodies to deliberate about use cases and safeguards, procurement teams that include a variety of functions so that those concerns can be repr

esented when technology is being considered, specific practices for higher impact use cases, pre-deployment testing, monitoring, human oversight, etc. And so I'm going to talk a little bit about, a little bit more in detail about what some of those practices are that, that enable the type of work that I think we heard from the other panelists. So first, know, you before considering what domains AI should be used in, it's worth considering in a particular context, is AI really the solution at all

? The answer does not have to be yes. It can be considered, but it is something that should be considered in the context of, is is there, there a fit for purpose here? Is is the, the agency or organization prepared to do this? Do they have the technical staff or at least understanding who can work with with external vendors? Is there sufficient data? Is the data in a clean and reliable format such that it can be used for AI systems? Is there evidence that this solution is effective for the parti

cular use case, whether that's a purpose-specific tool or a general-purpose tool? Is there— are there indications that it's appropriate for use in the domain that's being contemplated? And then the context-based risk assessments. After considering the potential use case and who might it impact, do the risks fall on subsets of the population inordinately in a way that, that wouldn't align with the government's mandate? So in the procurement process, some of the ways to manage, manage some of thes

e risks, obviously this is all easier if you're building it yourself, theoretically. And when you're procuring it, it's even harder. But so one of the things that ultimately needs to happen is that requirements need to extend to vendors. That can happen through contract language that ensures compliance with any risk management practices that the government needs to comply with. That might include contract terms that address privacy, testing and monitoring, performance standards, which all makes

sense if you think about it. A challenge that generative AI general-purpose tools are introducing is that the government might have procured a tool that is a standard general-purpose tool, word processing, data analysis, etc., when suddenly an AI component is available for that tool or is introduced into that tool. If that wasn't accounted for in the original contracting process, that can make managing the risks of that new component challenging, especially if it's turned on without the knowledg

e of, of the agency or the accountable folks within the agency. So the best case scenario is that tools where there might be an introduction of AI, that AI capabilities are off by default with notice and enterprise controls to determine whether and how to roll out AI capabilities with versioned updates and clear channels for feedback to, to the provider. The opposite is AI appears at random, is updated on the fly, and changes in an unpredictable way with no ability to turn it off. Certainly, tha

t's, I think, not a situation anyone wants to find ourselves in. The next step I think we heard quite a bit of was on risk management and how to make sure that high-risk or high-impact systems, AI systems in consequential contexts, contexts are subject to heightened requirements. In order for that to happen, there are some basic components that need to be in place. Firstly, structured inventory of the tech and AI-enabled systems that are in use at all so that those can be subject to the same req

uirements. Unfortunately, this seems obvious but is very often not in existence in enterprises and large organizations. Secondly, you need a process to determine if a new use case falls into those into the categories that have been defined. Again, seems obvious, doesn't exist unless it's it's been, been created. So a process to identify when a new use case for AI is being contemplated and to deliberate about whether it falls into any of those categories and to discuss whether there are any exemp

tions or special conditions that might apply. So such a process requires somewhat defined set of conditions under which an AI system would be required to go through some heightened safeguards. And that might include, as folks are saying, a definition of high-stakes decisions. It could include, you know, topical areas. For instance, in the memos from the OMB, some of the examples we're seeing are critical infrastructure, physical systems, healthcare, law enforcement, public benefits, employment.

Now, not every use case in all of those domains are those consequential automated decisions that sometimes we think about. And yet I would posit that at the moment it's too difficult to know what use cases in those domains are not high risk to create carve-outs preemptively. It is something that I think over time you can ascertain that, you know, text processing within the employment context is maybe not as high risk as facilitating decisions about who to interview. But then again, my colleagues

and I did some work a while back on the fact that just because things appear to be low risk does not necessarily mean that they present no risks or that they might not feed into some of those higher risk decisions. So even things that seem simple, like summarization, if they're used in one of those domains that tends to be higher risk, it's possible that they could cascade into, into contexts that people would want to have subject to heightened deliberation. So over time, that, that list of dom

ains might end up being refined, but having a defined list in the first place is going to be important. Having some parameters of what should be contemplated about a high-risk context before deploying AI is necessary. So what would an impact assessment look like? That might include intended purpose and expected benefit of an AI system, the quality and appropriateness of the data, the potential impacts of errors in that system, and whether there is oversight, recourse, you know, manual backup if

that system were to go wrong, and in certain cases, the results of independent review or auditing of a system to make sure that it's functioning. You'll— organizations often also want to develop a menu, so to speak, of mitigations for common risks so that when certain systems are kind of popping up often, certain types of systems, systems, it can become clear whether there are requirements that are necessary in all cases. For example, certain security characteristics, certain privacy protections

, certain types of tests that always need to be run. This can help facilitate a more streamlined review process over time. But as I think we've heard earlier, especially these more advanced systems or more, more unpredictable systems, it can be difficult to replicate tests. So we're not there yet, but we can start generating the evidence, building out a sort of playbook of common processes and what interventions are most often recommended by internal and potentially external experts. And I think

it's important to remember that even if you do everything right in risk management, high-risk use cases are identified, risks are enumerated, impacts are measured, mitigations are applied, there are still cases where the systems won't end up working, will still go wrong, will still lead to bias, discrimination, other types of harms. And there was an example of this recently in Amsterdam where they really went, you know, by the book, did, dotted all their i's, crossed their t's, worked with expe

rts, internal, expert, external, all the best practices. And they still found that the system was exhibiting impermissible levels of discrimination and bias in a welfare context.. And so just because you have the process in place doesn't mean that risks will be mitigated, but having the process in place certainly means that they have the opportunity to be mitigated, which I think is what we all hope for, that we can unlock the benefits of this technology as we learn more about how it works. So a

couple of challenges that, that sort of those basic contours of risk management experience when it comes to general purpose tools to keep in mind. So as Suresh mentioned, tests are not necessarily entirely reliable. You can't just test a system and then say it looks good, let's go. Tests can be different depending on if you do it multiple times. The way you set up tests of these generative systems can change the outcomes in ways you can't predict. And my team actually conducted testing on a var

iety of different LLMs and found that tests that purport to measure the same thing actually resulted in opposite conclusions. And so you really have to have an understanding of what you're testing and what the results of that test might indicate to feel confident that those tests should be relied on. Another challenge is that for LLMs and advanced AI systems, minor changes can dramatically change the risk profile. So if you customize an off-the-shelf LLM for a particular domain, that can have si

gnificant impacts on the safety characteristics. And that we found out through the same testing that I just mentioned. We were trying to understand how fine-tuning of systems changed underlying security and safety assumptions. And the challenging fact is that they do. And so having a clear process to keep track of changes to systems that are conducted or requested to determine when additional risk management practice is necessary is a key part of a system. And it's also important, I think we did

n't talk about this yet, that AI systems are typically not just one big model. I think Aaron mentioned this. They're increasingly calling tools in the background and, and leading to, you know, a complex scenario where, where the LLM is just an interface to databases, to the web, In some cases, these tools can take defined actions or undefined actions. And so these these are, are more complex circumstances than many AI governance frameworks in the public sector currently contemplate. And so somet

hing to keep a close eye on is when vendors are claiming that they can provide agentic systems or systems that can take action and call tools, these things are going to have a much different risk profile than just, um, the models themselves, which even with all of their challenges can at least be somewhat, uh, interpreted and understood in, insofar as testing how they might operate when they connect with a lot of tools in the wild. That, that makes it even, even harder. Um, so how do we handle s

ome of these things? Just a couple high-level recommendations. Um, policies around use for government and personal accounts. There's a lot of challenges in the private sector with shadow AI, where if there isn't a formal policy around AI use, people will just use their personal accounts to do some of the productivity type of tasks that they think might be low risk but actually might have an impact. So having a policy at the very least, an inventory of existing systems and whether they include AI

, what AI's purpose is, to the extent you're adopting these large-scale AI systems, doing it through enterprise tools to ensure that, you know, there's the ability to update at a reasonable cadence and not just sort of have updates come on the fly. Like I said, minor updates can lead to major workflow changes, major risk changes. So having visibility into whether there— when there are changes is critical. There is the ability to put in sort of customized safeguards. So preventing tools from resp

onding to queries of certain types that might be relevant if you want to make sure that your ordinary kind of government worker doesn't inadvertently turn to an AI system in a domain for which it's not permitted. Those aren't going to be perfect, but they can provide some blunt safeguards. Continual monitoring of these tools as they're deployed, because even if you do upfront testing, models can drift and change over time. They might interact with real-world data and scenarios, and it unpredicta

ble way. And start to think about use cases that can be tested robustly and maybe pre-cleared, because one of the unfortunate realities is that when everything is considered high risk, nothing gets the attention that it deserves. And so you really, you do want to think about what are the systems that require the most due diligence, and more so than others, so that, you know, people don't feel like everything is subject to heightened scrutiny in a way that they try to avoid process rather than go

ing through process. And, you know, I'll close my remarks saying that advancement in this area is quite jagged. So sometimes things will seem very capable, tests might seem very promising, and they in fact might be very useful and effective in a particular context. That does not mean that that capability is easily portable to another context, whether adjacent or more distant. Each use case should be considered independently and whether it's fit for purpose, whether it can provide sufficient expl

ainability, and whether it functions in the intended context. Because these are— while they are billed as general purpose, they're currently not necessarily generally effective. Thank you. Thank you very much. Yeah, I mean, it sounds like a lot of these, these AI tools are more work than they sound like they offer. One day you just have an AI that's just a bro, and then you have Mecha Hitler the next day. And then that could really upset a lot of the decisions that are being made if they're maki

ng these kinds of massive changes or even small changes in the background and that tool is being used. That can really disrupt a lot of the things. And it's hard to trace back where things actually were working and when they're not. So I think that's, that's an important fact to look at. I like to look at the Omniscience Index, and I go to the artificialanalysis.ai website, and they rate it on a positive 100 to -100, meaning that if it's— the more positive, the more correct and less hallucinatio

ns it has.. And only 4 are above 0, the highest being 13. And all of the other ones are not that good. They're all negative. And that's really kind of what the state of AI really is. It's very, very imperfect. And this index does shift over time and has gotten into the positive recently, which is yay, all right, very you good, know, hallucinating maybe a little bit less. But there's still a lot of work to be done and there's a lot of caution to be had. Any questions for, uh, for Ms. Bogan or any

body else? We really appreciate all your time today to be with us, and we'll have this recording for, for people to listen to later on. And maybe we'll, we'll see if we can ask you to come back at some other point to help, help, uh, do some other presentations to help people understand this a little bit better. Because we need more people to hear these kinds of, uh, informative talks about what's at risk and what the state of this whole, uh, thing is. Because we're making a lot of big decisions

right now, and There's a lot of money being put into it, and there's a lot of overpromising. There's a lot of peer pressure to adopt these products, and we have to make decisions on, on how we're going to have this be interacting with the people we represent. And these are big decisions, and we appreciate all of your helpful advice and your, your knowledge on this. So thank you very much. We appreciate your time today. All right, Miss Falco, anything else we need to accomplish for this meeting?

TPVs are initiated through a formal complaint filed by a community parole officer The complaint documents alleged violations and is submitted

to the Colorado State Parole Board for a review and disposition. The Colorado State Parole Board determines whether a violation occurred and what, if any, sanctions or corrective actions are warranted. Non-compliance that gives rise to the filing of a formal complaint varies widely in severity and is tied to statutory mandates and some instances. e wherever we can contractors with FTE because they're less expensive and they're more agile. I also want to recognize that some of the admin is going up because it has the ability to control our claim trend, which again is the 96%. So if we go up by a little bit on admin but we're driving down some of the claim trends where we have real big outliers, so ABA/PBT is an area where we're just going to have to put in more circumstances. NEMT, we had massive differences in how we credentialed, but it

pulled down our trend dramatically and we've got a negative trend going on. So we will continue to do those things and continue to be transparent and continue to work with our partners. Now if we could go to question 154, please. You asked about forecasting. So the department has sophisticated forecasting systems and methodologies and a strong track record. 11 of the last 15 years on this slide, you can see them, forecast was within 1% of the actual expenditures. So forecasting is by its very n

ature for healthcare, it will never be a perfectly precise science given the inherent challenges, including the complexity costs of healthcare, the volatility of the economy and its downstream impact on the unemployment rate, churn in the Medicaid program, forecasting by population due to the federal match, and challenging federal policies like the Affordable Care Act or the Public Health Emergency Continuous Coverage or the unwind, and soon the marketplace exchange tax credits and HR-1 requirem

ents, work requirements, and every 6 months. That said, We have continued to evolve our forecasting methodologies, recognizing $780 million in reductions, boy, we need to be right. So we have policy people working with data people working with finance people to make— to pull all those individuals together to make sure as these adjustments are going through that we refine those skills. Let's go to the next slide, please, and the next question. In question 154, you asked how we expanded eligibilit

y and benefits over the last few years. So over the last 7 legislative sessions, 2018 to 2025, the General Assembly has enacted more than 50 bills expanding eligibility for Health First Colorado, uh, or Medicaid, and the Children's Health Insurance Program. The slide summarizes it, but in your actual answer you can see 2 different lists that are each 3 to 4 pages. So while we truly celebrate this and we are so grateful for all the expansions, it is concurrent with about a 19% trend. So we're Fol

lowing that Medicaid sustainability framework, we are recognizing where we're getting unintended consequences and trying to pull back where that makes sense to address our trends. If you go to question 156, please, you asked, how would the proposed legislation to reduce the— Madam Chair, you asked, how would we reduce the claim cost trend growth? How would that target work? Can we actually cap an entitlement program? How would that work? So the administration proposes to establish a spending tar

get that creates predetermined— a predetermined goal and better alignment between HCPOF and the General Assembly in managing Medicaid expenditures in '27-'28 and beyond. It also establishes more transparent expectations across stakeholders. The governor's budget proposes that a target of 5.6 in fiscal year '27-'28 This factor aligns with the Medicaid general cost trends averaging a more sustainable 6% annually between 2015-16 and 2018-19. This compares to the unsustainable cost trends that avera

ged between 12% and 26%, or that 19% over the 4-year period. The administration proposes the spending target more closely parallel TABOR growth in out years, and that was about 4.4%. We recognize what a challenge that would be. In the same way, we have worked to align all of us around the sustainability framework quite successfully. We are working to align a target that we can all agree on, which will create expectations for the General Assembly and for Medicaid and for all stakeholders of what

we can afford as a system and what we cannot afford and cannot be addressed. This initiative would also create a more appropriate distribution of available general fund across all departments and the General Assembly priorities and address our reality, which is Medicaid cost trends are crowding out the rest of the state budget. We would welcome— this is a JBC bill. The bill would not impede HCPOF's over-expenditure authority. We would continue to have over-expenditure authority as all entitlemen

t programs under our domain do. It would simply establish a point of agreement on what we see as reasonable as we go forward. Go to the next question. Question 157 is about the criteria used to determine that administrative reductions would be limited versus very large trims and very large cuts around services or general benefits. So given the budget situation, HICPuff is required to propose significant expenditure reductions. This has not been easy on us. It is not easy It is not easy on our pr

oviders and is not easy on our members or stakeholders. Again, with 96% going to providers, that's where we needed to focus. The remaining 4% of the admin cost is 0.59% is our FTE, and again, we've gone out to all our contractors to see what we can do where that's reasonable. Again, not our counties. We're increasing money to counties for the HR1 that's before us. Most of the department's admin pays for systems necessary. We can't turn off systems. We can drive greater efficiencies. Again, we've

talked about Deloitte and the federal government helping us there. We are working on HCBS admin as I committed to, but going back to yesterday isn't where we want to be. We want to be the organization we are now, hitting that vision of equal to or better services and supports to low-income and people with disabilities while we work to find those areas, understanding what the providers see and understanding what our members see. Now we're on the team to do that. Let's go to the next. Question, a

nd I'm going to turn this over to our budget director Nancy Dolson, uh, to the next set of questions. Great, thank you, Director Bimsteifer. Nancy Dolson again. In questions 158 through 165, you asked more about HCPOF budget reductions and administrative funding, and this slide summarizes those responses, and more details are in your packet beginning on age 168. We have to propose reductions given the current context. Over the last decade, Medicaid costs have grown significantly faster than the

general fund revenues, and without action, uh, this trend increasingly crowds out funding in other state priorities. In meeting that requirement, HICPUS priority has been to preserve access to core benefits and coverage for our populations, and we've been intentional so that the populations who rely on our care receive the services they need. We have focused strategically on specific areas to bring costs in line with industry standards. Taking action now helps avoid more disruptive reductions in

the future. These proposals address the immediate need to address the budget shortfall while building a sustainable and effective system for the future. HICFA, we look forward to continue to partner with the General Assembly to meet constitutional budget requirements. In question 158, the committee asked us to provide an updated graph for department administration, and we've done so. Again, that'll be on page 168 of your packet. Overall, total payments for administration, including the RAE paym

ent, represents 4.5% of the total general fund appropriations for HCPOF while excluding Um, excuse me, when excluding the RAE administrative payment, the department administration is only 3.17% of general fund appropriations in this current fiscal year. In question 159, you asked us about administration related to the hospital provider fee. By law, the hospital provider fee administrative costs are restricted to 3% of its total expenditures from the provider fee cash fund, and over the years we'

ve come in between 2 and 2.6%. The administration cost under Chase is used to pay the administrative changes associated with covering more than 420,000 Coloradans, um, under our Medicaid and CHIP expansions and under the Medicaid Buy-in Program for Persons with Disabilities. This includes claim processing, eligibility systems, and counties who process applications and renewals. It includes member and provider call centers, compliance, and so forth. While HCPUF and all organizations should focus

on managing administrative costs, I want to underscore that there is no health plan, as Kim just mentioned— excuse me, Director Bimsteffer— in the state with administration in the 2 to 3% range. The larger focus that we have is on managing claim trend under Chase and all of Medicaid, which will thereby reduce the upper pressure on Chase and indeed all of Medicaid, which is further complicated due to HR 1. And question 1. Thank you, Madam Chair. I, I do appreciate the graphs or the bar charts, qu

ite honestly, with absolute dollars, but I, I know for me it would help if you could also put those as it relates to administration from a percentage standpoint? Has the, for instance, the 3.17 excluding the raise, is that up, down, where is it? I can't pick that up from a bar chart that has absolute dollars. Um, so as we dive in to find where our opportunities are and attack that with full force, um, let's, uh, share those percents, uh, with you in follow-up. Thank you, Representative Taggart.

Great, thank you. In question 160, the committee asked about our general fund appropriations, um, for administration, how they've been growing over the years. Um, as you just mentioned, Representative Taggart, we provide a detailed breakdown in our written response. We'll follow up with those percentages. In short, our appropriations have grown because the General Assembly and the federal government have asked us to do more, and because our top expenditure systems and IT are growing as they are

across the industry. For example, the growth we've experienced in personnel is primarily due to the implementation of new state laws and federal compliance. We've also seen growth in our technology costs Even though our systems come with very high federal match rates, we've still seen significant increases in our cost to run the systems and implement new initiatives. The other large driver of increases in administrative costs is the funding we provide to counties to determine eligibility. The Ge

neral Assembly has made significant investments in county administration since fiscal year '18-'19, not including temporary increases during the PHE unwind. In question 161, the committee asked us about how we've looked for administrative efficiencies before deciding that provider rate cuts were necessary. Again, because 96% of our expenditure goes to pay directly for care, as Director Bimsepter said, the size of the state's deficit means that there is no way to meet the fiscal pressures through

administrative spending. At the same time, as Director Bimsteifer mentioned, we have asked our contractors to propose reductions in their rates and scopes of work, and we're in the process of evaluating those proposals to put them into effect. We're also, as you know, working with the Department of Human Services on modernizing and reforming our county administration and technology systems to create efficiencies. And we still have to navigate the reality that the largest portion of our admin is

for systems And we can't eliminate those. We can't eliminate claims systems, eligibility systems, nor our analysis and reporting. Further, many of our administrative— Sorry, before you continue, Representative Brown's got a question. Absolutely. Thank you, Madam Chair. You note in your 10-year— at the very beginning, I'm sorry, I'm slow— the 10-year average growth rate is 8.8%. You're proposing that the growth rate come down to something more like the TABOR cap, obviously. If we were to— if, le

t's just say, we were to achieve that, what does that mean in terms of overall, like, the amount of money that we would be— how much money is that, I guess, that we're basically needing to cut in order to be in alignment with sort of the proposed growth rate. Does that make sense? Director Bimstecker. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Representative Brown. I don't have the numbers off the top of my head. We can bring them back to you, but the original trend without the $526 million in initial c

uts was about 11%, and we got it down to 7.7%. Some percent, and then we came up with another 200-plus to get that to that 780 or so total in reduction. So let's follow up with exactly what those percents are now. And Director Dolson, anything to add to that? Yeah, thank you, Director Bremsefer, and thank you, uh, Representative Brown, for the question. The thing that I would add to that is our fiscal year '26-'27 budget proposal, between, um, the, um, the request The R6 request and our budget a

mendment number 7 are targeted with a 5.6% growth in general fund. So those are the types of reductions that you're seeing before you is to bring that in line with the proposal. Representative Brown. Thank you very much. And I appreciate that very much. I think it's important. I recognize that Medicaid is the largest cost center that we have in the state budget. And it has been growing at a very steep rate. I just would say that not that you represent other departments necessarily, but I would a

lso say that if we are going to have this kind of a sort of a ceiling on growth, if you will, in Medicaid, I would I would argue that we should apply that to all departments. And I would make that request of the governor's office. Medicaid obviously serves some of the most vulnerable people. And I think it would be only appropriate that if we are expecting the most vulnerable, the most low-income people in Colorado to shoulder this burden, that everyone should shoulder that burden in the same wa

y. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Representative Brown, for your comments and sharing your perspective, and certainly noted. I'll note as we talk about administrative costs that there are many of those administrative costs are designed to reduce spending in other areas through things like prior authorizations, implementation of reductions, income verification technology, and fraud prevention. And if we were to reduce those types of things, that would actually cause our claims to increase

by a greater multitude. So, you know, these administrative costs, we need to really administer the healthcare program well. And as Kim has also mentioned, we are not done yet. We're going to continue to look at admin and look forward to continuing conversations with you as well. In question 162, you asked about CHIP expenditures and what appeared to be a— oh, I'm sorry. Thank you, Madam Chair. Your explanation was fine. You don't need to go through it. I understand there was a technical error a

nd you gave new numbers. No need to take it any further for me. Great. Thanks, Representative Taggart. And we regret the error. Thank you. In question 163, the committee asked us about additional federal funds we were able to draw on emergency services for non-citizens. In total, we think that would have been— we would have received about $6.6 million in additional federal funds per year, which is about 0.3% of the federal funding we've drawn for expansion members. As soon as we recognized the o

pportunity, we took We went forward to claim the federal funds back as far as we are allowed, which is 2 years. The hospital provider fee is the appropriate source of the state share because these members are ACA expansion members and the hospital provider fee statute specifically directs us to use that fee for expansion populations. In question 164, you asked us about the return on investment in our technology spending. I think this was a question from you, Representative Taggart. Developing an

ROI is a regular part of our approach to IT, but most of our technology spending is for claims that determine eligibility, pay claims, or host our claims data to enable analysis and the like. Other ancillary systems help case management agencies manage care for people with disabilities, connect infrastructure, and more. I think that Marfona Friend has a, a response to an earlier question we'll get to in just a moment. We're required by a series of federal laws and regulations to make sure we're

being efficient, that our systems work together, that they're economical, and that they're effective. CMS has robust methodologies to measure and verify that, and when we're able to demonstrate that, we receive that higher federal match rate, up to 90% for system design that helps offset our cost of building and running these systems, and 75% federal match for CMS-certified systems. Representative Taggart. Thank you, Madam Chair, and I appreciate again the answer to, to that question. I guess t

his is where, um, this subject is significantly different than what we see in private enterprise. And we don't see in a fiscal note, for instance, on a new investment of what that could in fact save us over a period of time. So it's not only ROI, but what the savings that are built into it, we see the cost of the upgrade, the software and hardware, and we see the number of FTE, but when you sit in one of the committee meetings and say, ultimately, is this saving us money, you get a lot of blank

stares. And that just would never happen in private enterprise. If you couldn't provide that information, it would it would never, never get approved. And that's where my frustration on this subject comes, is that we add and we add and we add to to the, the software and hardware, but never do we see the savings, which ultimately is what creates your ROI, obviously. Director Bimsteffer. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Representative Tigert. So you and I come from a long history of that. I'm us

ed to standing in front of people that get paid a lot more than me to give them— show them a break-even, right, period, a payback period, a return on investment. And you're competing with your peers to get the limited funding that is available. The— one of the biggest difference here that I had to open my mind to is who is this federal government and why are they giving us 90% on the dollar? I just— I had never seen anything like it. So there's a There's this Mama CMS that has extraordinarily ri

gorous tools because they're paying that 90% on all these systems that go forward. So I've had to learn to sort of adapt to this. Where's my payback period? Where's my— because somebody else is bringing in that 90% and we're bringing in the 10%. So for the most part, pretty much everything gets a great return for the state. It's just how much can you afford to do at once. And when we had— when they mandated we move to modularization all at once, that is something that I sort of shook my head at.

Wow, we have to build 19 systems at once and switch at once and add a system integrator at once during COVID where all of that inflation was going on, especially in IT. And this was really a hard period of time. So I would say maybe we need to do a better job of moving away from what what you and I would talk about as a payback period and a break-even period, and move into what's our cost, what's the return for the money that we are putting up, and do a better job of getting that to you. Let's

make that commitment going forward. Vice Chair Bridges. Thank you, Madam Chair. You know, as I think about the enormous cost the federal government will have to bear for all of these IT changes, the cost we have to bear for these IT changes, all in order to stop something that wasn't happening, which was a bunch of ineligible people who were working too much getting Medicaid coverage. There's no evidence that this was a widespread issue anywhere in the country, certainly not here. It seems that

just the— will the hurdles that are artificially created by HR 1 that just make people not want to deal with it and then lose their healthcare for that reason, will there be that many people people just bailing to make up for the cost to Medicaid for this, because certainly those people bailing are going to get sick and go to hospitals. So this is very, very bad for our medical system on the whole. I think it will dramatically increase insurance rates. This is overall dramatic increase in cost.

But even just in Medicaid, if we're just looking at Medicaid, the cost for all of these systems upgrades, especially on the timeline that the federal government has created. Is there actually any savings in all of this? Director Bimsteifer. The cost for the 5 years on our advance planning document was about $56 million. So the Fed has already approved about $25 million, roughly, a little more than that, for the first 2 years, which is all they approve. And they have already provided 90% back to

us. So that's already out the door, and we are 1.5% of the population across this country. And when you look at the Congressional Budget Office's savings, 75% and more of the savings to provide a tax break are because people lose coverage. And that is horrifying. And so we are swimming upstream to do the best we can to implement every system, every way that we can to get people back on, because it's one thing to fill out an application. It's another thing to take an action to go volunteer, to to

get that job, to go back to school. These are very difficult actions that people have to take. So this is going to be hard. And again, there isn't generally— for all of those work requirements and every 6 months, there isn't really general fund savings at all. To Senator Imobili's question, it's chase dollar savings, which reduces the pressure, as Director Dolson said, on the chase monies available. But we want to push that pressure back on because we need to get these people back on. They're l

iterally— lives are at stake, right? So we said the providers will have uninsured, uncompensated care, we'll have people that cannot get care for chronic conditions, whether it's diabetes medications or heart disease medications. We will have deaths. So we've got to avoid that. And we're going to have a hit to the economy. So let's see how fast the federal government maybe takes their foot off the gas and says, wow, I shouldn't have done that. We hope that that's going to happen, but let's see.

Then there's a gap in the Congressional Budget Office's forecast. Thank you, Madam Chair. I, you know, the, the thing is, we know this is going to hit hospitals really hard because there's going to be a ton of uninsured people showing up in the, uh, EDs, uh, looking for care. And the, the history of this national government is that anytime there are large corporations in trouble, they come to bail them out. So my guess is the overall cost for all of these changes, even to the federal government,

yet alone just to our healthcare system, is going to be enormous, and we will fundamentally see no savings but in fact massive increases in spending. Your whole presentation on this has just been utterly disappointing in the decisions that have been made by HR1. So thanks. So, Madam Chair, there's one last question that they're good on. I think Director Bates, you sent the info and everybody's good. Thank you. Oh, Director Gillison. Okay. Okay. So last question, 165. The committee asked us what

it should consider in terms of making investment in technology. I think we had a good dialogue on there, but I will add we are actively pursuing several initiatives for the committee and the General Assembly to consider through budgeting requests, including technology to reduce manual document reviews, which we talked about today in the ACR, a conversation on eligibility mitigating provider overbillings in high-risk areas like the ABA or PBT or NEMT for outlier provider billings through prepaym

ent reviews on claim edits, post-claim edits, so upping our game, fraud, waste, and abuse, and overbillings to maximize revenue streams at the provider level. And the committee will see more about these initiatives as we go through briefings and supplementals next week. Madam Chair, we have two choices. We can move into the Rural Health Transformation Program, or we can conclude. It's up to you. We're ready to go towards Rural Transformation if you'd like. Well, here's the thing. I don't think w

e have extra time in our schedule to add another day. I know this is of interest to a lot of people, so, you know, I wonder if you might just do your best to be brief and also, you know, share with folks what, if any, role the legislature has in this whole process, and then just sort of the highlights of what's coming to Colorado. Okay, Madam Chair, let's do that. Okay, we're going back. Joe, if you could take us back to the slides, we're going back to question 90. So I'll just celebrate as Joe

gets us to the right slide. CMS announced on December 29th that Colorado was awarded $200 million a year for $1 billion over 5 years. We are absolutely delighted. That has exceeded our expectations. On question 90, Rep. Brown, you asked how we engaged with other states. When you have a competitive grant like this with other states, we actually don't disclose that. We did a ton of stakeholdering, but we did not actually push that out. So our approach was to do a ton of stakeholdering individually

as well as in these pretty big meetings, but we did not disclose what we did do. Let's go to slide 91. We did take in all the feedback you asked. Did we look at— I said slide 91, I meant question 91. Did we listen to our rural hospital partners in a risk written answer, we actually provided every suggestion that they provided and which ones we adopted. Some we could not adopt. To your base question, Madam Chair, this has been stages of grief. We have had people that are rural CEOs who have foug

ht for the better part of a decade of their last career trying to get the federal government to step up to rebuild them a chassis because their hospitals are built in the '50s. And so their expectation was this would be massive monies to be able to rebuild hospitals, and it's not allowed to do that. Um, Chase money helps give our rural hospitals just base increases in payment, pays significantly more than we would have otherwise, and this is not what the Rural Health Transformation is for. So we

've been through stages of grief. There are others that are welcome to the money. It's also behavioral health providers that are the old CMHCs. It's emergency medical services. Its clinics as well. So we've been through stages of grief, and as people get it, they come more along for the ride. And then on question 92, why was the final Rural Transformation Program not fully shared? We said the first part, but what we did do— you know, what did we do to make sure key stakeholders knew what was goi

ng in there? We actually sent early a complete submission over to the Colorado Rural Health Center We have been joined at the hip with the Colorado Rural Health Center, so we shared that a couple days in advance of its due date. We were submitting it on the 4th of November to make sure we didn't miss the 5th deadline, and then we had a working session with them to review all of their changes and to implement those that did not conflict with CMS requirements or prohibitions. For those not familia

r with the Colorado Rural Health Center, it's Colorado's not-for-profit Office of Rural Health. The CRHC works with federal, state, and local partners to offer services and resources to rural healthcare providers, facilities, including hospitals, and communities. Diverse insights, knowledge, they're in our mind best in show with boots on the ground and the best data in the system, which we use that data in partnership with them to put forward such strong proof points of who we were caring for an

d why we should get this money as a state. The CEO of that organization is Michelle Mills. She's also the president and the National Rural Health Association. So that's the organization that we really partnered with because they're so focused on the rural. And then for the next slide, I'll hand it over to Budget Director Nancy Dolson for questions 93 through 96. Very good. Thank you, Director Bimsteifer. Nancy Dolson here again. Looks like I'm on the correct slide there. For— in question 93, the

committee asked how the rural health transformation funding can be used to stabilize rural hospitals. Hospitals. While there are a lot of, you know, strings attached from the federal government and the funding cannot be used as direct, no-strings-attached grants, there are a number of initiatives in our approved application that could be helpful for hospitals. Our application included over $106 million directly related to sustainable access and over $150 million for workforce development initia

tives. None of the funding in our application is for administrative layers no state-driven regional structures, or the continuation of existing programs. And despite a 10% allowable administrative allowance, we've restricted our administrative spending to less than 3% of the total, which is necessary. We've got to have that for basic administration like application scoring, program monitoring, federal reporting, and is using funding to supplement or duplicate other state initiatives initiatives

is expressly prohibited. In question 94, you asked us about the risks of regionalization and centers of excellence. Sorry, it's getting late. Thank you. CMS prioritized programs that encourage collaboration between rural providers. We think this builds upon recent legislation from the General Assembly, including Senate Bills 23-298, which allowed for public hospital collaborative agreements, and Senate Bill 25-078, which allowed nonprofit hospitals to enter into collaborative agreements with oth

er health facilities. Those collaborative agreements means, you know, the ability to share reasonable high-cost administration and overhead, and those things really can plague our rural hospitals. So these are things like HR recruitment, training, acquisitions of supplies and drugs, IT management, prior authorization, quality assurance, and more. Second, the inclusion of Centers of Excellence in Colorado's grant does not prevent services from being provided, but rather provides additional resour

ces and assistance to improve care while supporting stronger regional collaboration. And bottom line, we do not believe that improving care and strengthening regional collaboration will result in the loss of local care. Chair. Representative Taggart. Thank you, Madam Chair. I guess the question I would pose is, with the advisory committee you're putting together now— and, and I realize for application purposes you relied on one very specific group that had a great deal of expertise. But going fo

rward, now that the application has been approved and the funds are moving, how prevalent are our rural hospitals on this advisory committee? Because I think you probably know we get the communications from our rural hospitals that aren't aren't as satisfied with this process as you may think they are. So how do we turn that around? Is the advisory council made up of a good number of those rural hospitals so you that, know, they feel a significant part of this? Director Bimsteffer. Thank you for

the question, Representative. We sent out a draft on the 23rd, I think it was, of December and asked for feedback by January 7th. We took in all that feedback and we had a more complicated— an advisory committee and an executive committee. We got feedback that thank you for trying to get as much input as you can, but it's too big and too complicated and it will take too long. So we sent in another one last week, which we should have back this week. And the initial comments are I think people ar

e happy with it. So it's only an advisory committee. The specific answer to your question is 4 rural hospitals, which then we got some poking from the other providers that they didn't have that many on. So we're doing the best to thread the needle as best we can, but it is more representatives than anybody else. And we even took out the votes from the state. We had 6 before, we now have 4, and none of them vote. And so we tried to spread the love with emergency medical services, clinics that are

out there, the rural hospitals who have the most voice in the room. But we still need to— everybody needs to remember, comply with what CMS needs us to do through the negotiations, and we have to meet those obligations or they will claw back and we have to spend in the periods. But we— I think we have the right. We'll know in a couple of days, but I think, sir, we've found the right balance. Thank you. Great. Thank you. In question 95, the committee asked us about an ensuring that decisions abo

ut what services remain open in rural communities stay in local control. And just would underscore again, there's no aspect of our Rural Health Transformation Program that would allow for any type of regional or centralized entity to make those types of decisions. Now we will move to your questions about rural provider payments. Next slide, please. All right. So this next set of questions begins on page 100 of your packet. In questions 96 and 97, you asked us about alternative payment, payment m

odel possibilities and how other states have used various federal flexibilities to stabilize funding. Um, we've created capitation to primary care providers, advanced value-based payments that now transcend more than 50% of all Medicaid payments, which is good news. Um, ultimately, any new payment methodology that does not increase total payments is not likely to alleviate the financial pressures these providers are facing. But they can help align goals around affordability, efficiencies, improv

e patient health and outcomes. Further, designing and piloting rural value-based care models is a core component of that Rural Health Transformation Program. And we will evaluate ideas and concepts as they come in and share ideas that we have with stakeholders. Providers, and we'll continue to pursue payment concepts that might give providers additional flexibility and stability. And with that, I'll hand that back to Director Bimsteffer. Madam Chair, members of the committee, that concludes our

remarks. We appreciate your patience and your partnership, and we're here for you as you go forward and make some very difficult decisions. Thank you very much for your time today. Thank you. Any last questions on the rural health transformation? $1,000. All right, thank you, thank you very much, uh, for all of your time today on HICPOF Day 2. Uh, that concludes the work of the Joint Budget Committee for the day. We will stand in recess until tomorrow.
