I'm excited to say that we we have reached a good middle ground, and we'll be bringing an amendment for seconds that addresses some of those concerns. And so I'm very excited that that was able to be worked out, and it also brings me joy. The greatest

thing, um, the greatest thing here is that we were able to engage people early on and also later on in the process and come to an agreement, and then have Rep. Badley join with this expertise. So I'm going to turn turn it over to her to speak to that. Representative Bradley. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Rep. Foray, for adding me on. I am needle certified, been doing it for over 10 years. So I want to talk to you guys a little bit, give you kind of the basics, because I think there's st

ill some confusion when it comes to it. We as practitioners go through a very extensive graduate-level coursework, so gross anatomy, um, you know, diagnosis, treatment, all of the things. But then to get certified in dry needling for physical therapists, you have to wait 2 years till you've been practicing to even get dry needle certified. The coursework is not you just go, they hand you needles and say, go get them. It is 50 hours of some of the most intensive classes I have ever taken. And I'v

e taken a lot because I've been a PT for 26 years. You're not guaranteed to pass the course if you're not competent. Course instructor is not going to say, yes, go provide pneumothoraxes for everyone that you treat. It is a very extensive course. You have to demonstrate competency for then the instructor to say, I'm going to allow you to do it. In fact, for PTs, you have to have a certain number of hours before you can move on to the next dry needling course, which is more extensive as well. I b

elieve that the OTs will be challenged to that same level. I've been a PT PT, like I said, for 10 years. I've never once had a major adverse reaction. And I wanted to go over what dry needling is in the physical therapy space because sometimes I believe there are turf wars and, and there's enough patients to go around. Dry needling for a PT has nothing to do with acupuncture except for the type of needle. It's an acupuncture-type needle that we all use. It's dry because we're not putting in lido

caine or any liquid type of medicine into the needle. For us, it goes into the trigger point of the muscle, scar tissue, ligaments, tendons, things that don't typically have blood flow, to induce blood flow and to induce the healing. Now, why that's important for our patients is because we don't want patients missing work. We don't want patients turning from an acute condition into a chronic condition. This gets people back to work more timely. And the effects— I wanted to read you a couple of d

ifferent effects They took a huge sample size of people. Large pain reduction effects were seen up to 24 weeks after dry needling. And this is from PubMed, which is a journal that most healthcare professionals consider the gold standard. 0 to 72 hours, there was a large effect of pain reduction, almost 81% after dry needling. And anything over 0.8 is considered a large effect in clinical research. Immediate and short-term pain reduction, often changed by 1.5 to 2.3 points. If you have a pain of

a 6 and it goes down to a 4 after dry needling, that's pretty significant. Patient-reported benefits: pain improved 74%, mobility improved 71%, gait improved 46%, strength improved 38%. 82% of respondents said they would recommend dry needling to others. And then let's talk about the adverse effects. Out of 21,000 patients, almost 36% reported bruising. Okay, you're gonna have some bruising. I mean, these are little veins that you're getting into. Bruising is to be expected, or soreness. And we

talk about these things with our patients. 20 major adverse events out of almost 21,000 treatments, which was 0.1%. I looked it up to see in the 9 states that allow dry needling. Is there any evidence that OTs had increased risks or adverse effects because they have been granted in their scope of practice to be allowed to dry needle? And there's not. They don't, they don't differentiate, which tells me this is very good. There's no evidence, published cases, state board sanctions, or legal judgm

ents showing that OTs performing dry needling have caused a higher rate of major adverse outcomes. OTs, I believe, like PTs, are trained for major gross anatomy, major physiology. We often differentially diagnose. We are direct access PTs, so before people even see doctors, they come to us. We do not want to hurt patients. We don't want to hurt our patients because they're our patients, but we don't want to be brought up on any kind of licensing issues as well. I believe— and I wanted to get on

this bill because I believe in rural Colorado we have deserts of practitioners, and I have sat at this Capitol for 4 years now to bring more PAs, more nurse practitioners, more of the medical professionals to the rural areas that I also represent in Douglas County, and I believe this is a very minimal risk versus huge reward way to get more practitioners in all of our districts to allow patients to get back to work, everything that we need to be able to do to, to live in the state and to help ge

t patients from the chronic— to not get them in the chronic stage, to keep them in the acute stage, which we consider anything for us is under 6 weeks, to get them seen as timely as possible. And the more practitioners we have offering this type of treatment, the better we can get patients. And I will tell you, we have a consent form at my clinic. We always talk because the number one question, what is the difference between this and acupuncture? We are not acupuncturists. We say it from the get

-go, acupuncture is a different type of modality modality most of the time, although they can treat pain like we can, but we are not trying to do what acupuncturists do. I am not changing your chi, your energy, your meridians. I have no clue how to do it. I refer to acupuncturists to do it. So we are not stepping on any toes, and I believe that OTs are very equipped to perform this modality. So thank you for your time and for listening. Thank you both. Do we have any questions from the committee

for our bill sponsors? Yes, Representative Stewart. Thank you, Madam Chair. Just, just going to ask this now to clarify. So we figured out the educational piece, Reps, with like with the upcoming amendment. Representative Frey. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for the question. Yes, one of the things that was concerned is that it was too broad. The intention of why it was broad was because the board and DORA were going to be working on those. We are going to bring an amendment that says that i

t is parity of what the PT is doing in terms of education, training, and course requirements. And if the board and DORA want to go higher in terms of that requirement, they can. That's up to them when they're stakeholdering. But this at least will explicitly say that parity. Thank you. Further questions? All right, seeing none, we'll move on to our witness testimony. Do you have a preference, Representative Ferray, on order? Okay, I will, um, then start. I will start with the folks that have sig

ned up against the bill. If you'll come forward, please. I have Jackie Shumway. I have Aaron Deterding and Cheryl Wheeler. Is there anyone else in the room that wanted to testify against the bill that I didn't call? All right. Oh, online. Cheryl Wheeler. So go— if you could pull up Cheryl Wheeler online. And I'll start with the gentleman in front of me since you're here in person. When you're ready, I'll have you turn your microphone on, which is that— you got it. Introduce yourself and who you

represent, if anyone,, and you'll have 3 minutes. Okay, um, good afternoon, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for this opportunity to speak on this issue today. My name is Aaron Dieterding. I'm a recent graduate of Colorado Chinese Medicine University and a board member of the Acupuncture Association of Colorado. I'm speaking today in opposition of House Bill 26-1042 as presented. I will say that I had the opportunity to talk with Representative Farré earlier, and I am in agree

ment with some of the amendments that we spoke about. There's a couple other points, or at least one other point that I wanted to bring up as well. I think it's important to note that while occupational therapists are— they do provide essential healthcare services. Dry needling is an invasive procedure that requires a foundation in needle-specific safety, which is not found in standard OT education. As written, this bill is missing the detailed rigorous training standards, and it continues to ex

pand on the practice of dry needling, which lacks clear statutory guidelines. In, in both of these cases, it creates immediate and unnecessary public risk. Again, we did address the, the hours of training. I think it's important to note acupuncturists like myself, I received 800 hours of supervised needling practice and nearly 400 clinical patient encounters before I could practice independently. I don't think it's reasonable to expect an occupational therapist or anyone else using dry needling

to go through this level of training. But I do think there needs to be a standard that's set, and I think that doing that in a collaborative— collaborative way with acupuncturists, physical therapists, chiropractors, MDs, anyone who's using this technique, I think that we could come together collaboratively and establish appropriate guidelines for that. I also think that that the current definition of dry needling according to the Code of Colorado Regulations and the Colorado Revised Statutes la

ck the clinical detail necessary to safely govern a growing group of practitioners for this modality. Also, I think that's something that we could work on collaboratively to come up with a standard for as we move forward and more people potentially want to use this modality in their practice. Um, yeah, that's all I have to say. Thank you. Thank you for your time and testimony. We'll go online to Ms. Cheryl Wheeler. Go ahead and unmute yourself and tell us who you represent. You'll have 3 minutes

. Wonderful. Thank you, and thank you, Chair and members of the committee, for allowing me to test concerning dry needling by occupational therapists. My name is Cheryl Wheeler. I've been a licensed— I've been a licensed acupuncturist, and I'm currently practicing in Westminster, Colorado. I also work as a clinical supervisor in the local acupuncture college. I oppose the bill as written, but as my colleague said, there's been some wonderful movement towards getting more clear amendments put in.

That help alleviate a bunch of my concerns here. My major concern is that dry needling is one of our most dynamic forms of needling techniques. It is very vigorous, and there is a lot of changes that happen in the muscle in a very short amount of time. To be able to accurately differentiate what is muscle, what is structure, you have to have a great deal of hands-on time as well as supervised clinical time so that when you find people in vulnerable populations, the elderly, the frail, the very,

very young, you have someone who is experienced and can help guide you through how to safely do these needling techniques on unique populations. And I acknowledge that most courses cannot cover everything at once. But if we are looking at using this and increasing the number of practitioners that can dry needle to help with these deserts of care in rural situations, it needs to have a robust clinical requirement that includes populations that aren't just athletes or aren't just working-class pe

ople, because people like your grandma are going to come and find us, and aging muscles, aging organs all react differently, and they all have a different kinesthetic feel. And I hope that as you consider this bill as it goes forward, you look at how much hands-on time occupational therapists spend with their patients versus other forms of counseling and environmental modification. And that you would choose an appropriate amount of hands-on clinical time so that they can safely gain these skills

of differentiation of, is this a tight muscle or is this a hypertensive artery or other major concerns? Um, again, thank you for my chance to speak, and, uh, thank you. Thank you, Ms. Wheeler. And next up is Dr. Amy Mager. Thank you, Dr. Amy Major. I am the Federal Advocacy Chair of the American Society of Acupuncturists. I serve on our dry needling task force, and I thank you, Chair, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee for the opportunity to speak with you. I also serve on t

he National Certification Board of Acupuncture and Herbal Medicine State Relations Task Force, and I want to applaud all of the efforts that have moved amendments forward. And my deepest hope is that this will continue and that this bill will become something that we can support and encourage other providers to learn about, because occupational therapists are amazing. They help people heal. They help people do things they couldn't do before. These are really important things. My deepest concern

and our deepest concern as the American Society of Acupuncturists as reflected in our dry needling position statement, is that there is currently no zero, zilch certification. Everyone who has taken a PT program or any other dry needling program has taken a certificate program. A certification requires a board above a board, just like the National Certification Board of Acupuncture and Herbal Medicine has a board over at the NCCA. Right? Physical therapists take the APT exam. OTs take a national

exam. Nurses take the NCLEX, and medical physicians take medical boards. These are not given by the person that taught the class. Our concern is the only exams that folks are taking are by the person that taught the class to them the night the class ends. As opposed to a third-party national certification, which all of us have taken for our other procedures to practice and to obtain licensure. So that's one deep concern that I have, and making sure that there are guardrails around adverse event

s, around guardrails around exact standards for training, because the ASA does not feel that 50 hours is enough. We would like to see the standards be more like the AAMA, the American Academy of Medical Acupuncture, which requires 300 hours and 100 hours of supervised clinical experience and a third-party exam, because this is how we keep patients safe. And that's the deepest goal, because we know with TJ Watts' most recent injury, which was performed not by an acupuncturist because acupuncturis

ts are not in that facility, that this is a very large man with large musculature. So either his likely brilliant P.T. made an error in length of needle, placement of needle, width of needle, or something else happened. But if it can happen to somebody who's that big, who has lost significant work and can't participate in the Pro Bowl, it can happen to any of us. And it's all about our patient care. Thank you so much. Thank you, Dr. Major, for your— thank you, Dr. Major, for your testimony. Okay

, I apologize and thank you for your patience. I was across the hall presenting a bill in Judiciary. Look, I want to open up for questions if any other— if we have any questions from the legislators. Rep. Johnson. Thank you, Madam Chair. Uh, this question's for Mr. Deterding. Sorry, I think I mispronounced that. But, uh, my question is, do you believe that physical therapists should be doing dry needling? I just want to make— um, yeah, I mean, I have no issue with any other practitioner doing it

. I think the big issue is what the training is to allow them to do it, to make sure that the patients are safe, also that the practitioners are safe, that they're protected from any kind of like legal issues that may arise from if there does happen to be an injury. I'm personally, I'm open to other practitioners getting the training to do this, to offer this to their patients as well, if that makes sense. Any other questions from the committee? I have one question for Dr. Major, um, and Again,

apologize if this was already addressed while I was gone, but wondering if you could talk a little bit about the process by which this— if this bill passes, then there's a timeframe before they go into rulemaking that if you— if acupuncturists would feel comfortable in that, that that rulemaking process would protect for any safety issues that might come about. Absolutely. We have to have complete faith in the legislature and the due diligence that you all do and the intention and attention that

you put into patient safety and best practices. Thank you. Okay. With no, no further questions, I think we can move on to the next panel. Thank you for your testimony. I'd like to call up the folks online. Um, I— we have one person in, um, sorry, two people in person, Mr. Evan and Dr. Molly. sorry, Oh, Mr. Evan Bowe and Dr. Molly Han Floyd. Wonderful, welcome. And then we'll also bring up the folks that are online. Mr. Brian Covert, Ms. Amanda Hoffman, Mrs. Stephanie Holst, and Dr. Rebecca Grif

fith, and Ms. Stephanie Holst. Oh, we got two Ms. Stephanie Holsts. Just the one, please, unless there are two. And then we also have a, um, for questions only, Ms. Monica Sutherland. Thank you. Wonderful. If you can state your name and who you're with and provide your testimony starting from left to right. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair and members of the committee. My name is Molly Hahn Floyd, and I'm the president of Occupational Therapy Association of Colorado. We were going to have a num

ber of people joining us yesterday as well, but just given all the changes, we're your team. So anyways, OTAC represents occupational therapy practitioners and students across the state of Colorado. Occupational therapists complete rigorous graduate-level education, earning either a master's or a doctoral degree, which typically requires 6 to 7 years of higher education and clinical training. Our practitioners work in a wide range of settings including hospitals, outpatient clinics, schools, hom

e health, mental health, pediatrics, older adults, and community health programs. Across all these settings, occupational therapy is focused on function, helping people participate in daily activities that matter most, such as self-care, work, school, and family life. We've heard from individuals across Colorado that patients are experiencing delays and disruptions in their care. This is because patients are currently required to seek another provider for dry needling when it's clinically approp

riate within an existing occupational therapy plan of care. This bill directly improves continuity of care. OTAC supports this bill because it improves patient outcomes by reducing delays, increasing access to care, as we've spoken, particularly in the Western Slope and Eastern Plains where healthcare professionals are limited, and allowing patients to remain within— with their established occupational therapy provider. Importantly, this bill includes clear and robust safeguards, including requi

red education overseen by an accreditation board, demonstrated competency written informed consent, and regulatory oversight through rulemaking. This is a safety-forward approach, and it mirrors existing requirements for physical therapists in Colorado. The American Occupational Therapy Association, our national professional association, supports the use of dry needling when it's clinically appropriate. Additionally, 9 other states already allow occupational therapists to perform dry needling. N

otably, the American Physical Therapy Association of Colorado also supports this bill. For these reasons, OTAC respectfully asks for your— for a yes vote. And thank you, Madam Chair and members of the committee, for your time and for your service to the people of Colorado. Thank you. Mr. Bowe. Thank Madam— thank you, you, Madam Chair and members of the committee. My name is Evan Bowe, and I'm an occupational therapy doctorate student with the Craig Creighton Regis Pathway in Colorado, and I'm he

re in support of HB 26-1042. In a master's or doctorate-level occupational therapy program like the one I am currently attending, we receive rigorous training in anatomy and physiology, clinical reasoning, and maintaining a strong focus on safety. This includes screening for contraindications and precautions, monitoring patient responses, and practicing patient-centered informed consent. My program follows strict accreditation standards set by the Accreditation Council for Occupational Therapy E

ducation. Patient safety is a foundational part of everything we are taught and to do in our clinical training. From my clinical learning experiences, I've also seen how pain and movement limitations can block function and how care can become fragmented when a patient has to navigate additional referrals or separate episodes of care to access a single modality. What I appreciate about HB 26-1042 is its structure. It doesn't treat dry needling casually. It links authorization to education, demons

trated competency, and written informed consent under regulatory requirements established through rulemaking. I respectfully ask for your support of HB 26-1042. Thank you for your time and consideration, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you. Ms. Sutherland. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Yet again, I am Monica Sutherland from the Division of Professions and Occupations in the Department of Regulatory Agencies, here for questions only. Thank you. And I th

ink we did miss one additional witness on the last panel that we'll bring up now. Is Ms. Schwemway in the audience? Wonderful. If you could join us while you are getting yourself situated, we'll move to to the folks online. Um, could Mr. Covert begin, please? Yes. Um, good afternoon, members of the committee. My name is Brian Covert. I am an occupational therapist, certified hand therapist, working in an outpatient setting serving patients of all ages who are recovering from upper extremity inju

ries. I have a master's degree in occupational therapy, 25 years as an occupational therapist, and over 10 years of practice as a certified hand therapist. I'm here to ask for your support of HB 26-1042. I was trained and certified in trigger point dry needling by Mild Pain Seminars in 2021. The total number of continuing education hours was 68 hours. The instructor was Jan Dommerholt, PT/DPT. This was advanced coursework built upon the foundation of anatomical knowledge and clinical reasoning r

equired in occupational therapy. Certification was earned by passing both written and practical tests. Of course, the practical test, you have to demonstrate the dry needling technique to various different muscles during that practicum. The skills necessary for successful trigger point dry needling include being able to find appropriate anatomical landmarks on the patient, palpate the involved muscle— that's really the key thing, is being able to palpate the muscle and find it Find the exquisite

ly tender part of the muscle denoting the top band in the muscle, and then the tender trigger point, followed by appropriately needling said muscle and the involved tissue, including the fascia. Knowing the pain referral patterns for each muscle is an additional component in assessing the patient and determining the appropriate tissue to needle. When I say pain referral pattern, what I mean is if you hit the trigger point in the you muscle, know, by palpating it, then it'll send the pain down th

rough the pain referral pattern that is consistent with what you would expect with that muscle. Functional activity always follows dry needling interventions. Safety was emphasized throughout. We received extensive and detailed training and risk management precautions, sterile technique, informed consent, all contraindications, and safe needling angles. Training included extensive practice on how to needle each muscle to appropriately. For instance, in the case of the pronator teres, you would i

nsert the needle then straight into the muscle, then turn the needle towards the inside of the elbow to avoid hitting the median nerve and vascularization. The phrase "if in doubt, stay out" was stressed throughout the coursework. The story of why this matters is a daily story, not a one-off. This happens all the time in clinic. Many of my patients have trigger points from overuse, from immobilization, from poor posture, or from trauma. When other manual therapy techniques, home exercise program

s and modalities, education, splinting, and job site modifications fail, dry needling can be an effective technique. Without access to this technique, the patients with tennis elbow, for instance, experiences more debilitating pain than necessary and therefore has difficulty lifting her grandchildren and performing her job at the computer. Putting her employment at risk. Not being allowed to use all the tools that we could as therapists makes more, more invasive and expensive interventions much

more likely. Allowing us to use the skills that we are certified to do is a responsible, no-cost, low-risk, high-impact improvement to patient care. Thank you, Mr. Covert. Thank you. Yes, thank you. Appreciate that. Dr. Griffith. Thank you, Madam Chair and members of the committee. My name is Dr. Rebecca Griffith. I'm a physical therapist and the president of the American Physical Therapy Association of Colorado. As a profession that currently utilizes dry needling, physical therapists welcome t

he addition of occupational therapists being able to provide this intervention. This is fundamentally an issue of patient access to quality care. No one profession owns a specific intervention, nor is anyone suggesting that clinician without the appropriate training perform dry needling. Occupational therapists have the baseline clinical expertise as a foundation for dry needling. As a profession that initially received significant scrutiny for the performance of dry needling, we are a case stud

y in success and we have no qualms about our colleagues. We respect the training of occupational therapists in combination with their clinical decision-making related to function, participation, and patient-centered outcomes. Allowing Allowing occupational therapists to incorporate dry needling as an adjunct to a comprehensive plan of care can reduce delays, improve function, and expand access, particularly in settings where patients may otherwise have to wait or go without services at all. Colo

rado's regulatory framework is strongest when it supports safe, timely access to care by enabling licensed caring professionals to practice to the fullest extent of their skill set in service of patients. Thank you for your time and consideration in promoting access to care for Coloradans. Thank you, Ms. Schwamme. All right, we're on now. Um, I am actually very pleased that we're able to talk today, but I've actually brought a packet to y'all. I'm representing Living Younger Longer Institute. My

husband is head of research at the Colorado Chinese Medicine University, and after coming back from China this last summer, I have— we run the Tai Chi a PhD project. And I know that sounds real nice, but it's a great thing. I realized how seriously the problems are getting around the country with people needing— more people needing to know how to do acupuncture. So I enrolled and went back. I'm going back to school at 66 years of age. Yay! And now I'm 67. So anyway, but I did start back knowing

at minimum that I have 28 months to go through. Now, I've taught as a professor. I've organized a lot of things. And I would never dream in a million years of going to a 2 or 3-day event even though my training was all in— I'm basically trained in physical therapy except on the prevention side. So I have a lot of that. I work with Health Sciences Center. I've done lots of things. But I know just like many of my colleagues that are currently in school with me that are full-blown doctors, MDs, co

ming back and becoming acupuncturists. And so I'm glad that we have put on some more training for this. But we really need to talk about what Oregon did, which is basically said you got to have a lot of acupuncture training in order to do this. Dry needling is acupuncture even if we say it isn't. We're not going to argue that point right now, but what I'm trying to say is there are some real things and it should be seen as a whole person health. My husband and I will be presenting at Oxford— I m

ean, sorry, Harvard in April on whole person health because of what we know about this and I would just encourage you to keep keep, as the others were saying, keep putting more guardrails so that we don't— so that we do improve people's care. And again, should it be one person, one profession doing it? Not necessarily. But I do think it's very important to understand that if you don't— you don't know what you don't know. And what I learned my first 2 weeks when I was there at school is it's pret

ty scary to stick one of these needles in. You better know what you're doing. You've got nerves. You've got so much that you have to worry about. Pneumothoracic collapse is really a concern. I will finally summarize this with there are many people who come and see my husband, have over the last 20 years that he's been practicing, along with others who have had dry needling issues. They don't report them because number one, they don't know about DORA, and and they— the second one is, is they just

flat out, it's too hard to report, and they've just had a tough time, so they let it go. And it's not life-threatening, it's just uncomfortable. And I will say the final last thing in the report, if you Notice what I gave you that was the big one. It's not pneumothoracic collapse, it's infection. And so we need to really look at this dry— I mean, the clean needle technique that we have to do, literally we spend one weekend testing just for as long as they're doing the entire dry needling initia

l certification. So those are just the reality of it. Please consider, you know, keeping this going in the right direction. Again, I welcome everybody to learn about acupuncture. And understand how incredibly wonderful it is. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Shumway. Um, any questions for this panel? Okay, thank you so much for your testimony. Thanks for those who are online, appreciate your time. Are there any other witnesses wishing to testify? That are in the audience? Okay, seeing none, the witness

testimony phase is now closed. Sponsors, do you have any amendments? No, we will be bringing them for seconds. Okay, thank you. If, um, committee, any amendments? No amendments. The amendment phase is now closed. Closing remarks from the sponsors. Uh, Rep. Bradley. Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm I'm trying, trying to be patient. Um, I just want to clear up a couple of things. Somebody had mentioned that, um, acupuncturists perform dry needling. They don't. They perform acupuncture. Physical therap

ists and OTs, hopefully in the state, will perform dry needling. A court case settled that. They perform acupuncture, we perform dry needling. A couple other things: infection is not a risk, a real risk. A 21,000-person study showed that adverse effects was pneumothorax, fainting, a couple other things. I've never in 10 years had a person have an infection. I don't even know how you would claim an infection with a 30mm needle versus a virus that you tend to have. And we, we get biopsies every da

y in this country for or kidneys, things like that. Those don't cause infections, neither would a dry needle. So I just wanted to put that on the record as well. Acupuncturists have 300 hours of training for acupuncture. That is their entire training. That is their entire modality, is to do acupuncture. Physical therapists and OTs provide a ton of other modalities, and I just wanted to go on the record with these are intensive courses. We do no clean procedures. We have to wipe the area with alc

ohol. We have to— the, the needles come in individual needle packets that you have to open and take out and unstick them with glue to then put them into the patient. And if anyone on here thinks that I would ever be on a bill that doesn't safeguard patients, then we need to go to coffee, because my whole intent here is to provide more access and public safety to my patients. I would never be on a bill that would not keep patients safe, especially in my field of practice. So thank you. Representa

tive Frey, good bill vote. Yes, uh, I, I think we covered a lot of ground, and I really appreciate some of your expertise that Rep. Bradley has brought to the table. I just want to thank the committee. You've brought some really good questions. You've been thoughtful about it, and so the holder engagement has been not only with the community members but also with you, and you've participated and leaned in and asked really great questions. So thank you, and I hope you're supporting it. One more t

hing, Representative Bradley. Thank you, Madam Chair. I will free needle anyone in here to show you guys it is not scary. It is not scary to put the needle in. Um, and if anyone wants to ask Representative Garcia and some other people that I have dry needled here, and I will happily me after you sign a consent form. Do that for all of you. Thank you. I think that we need to move the bill now. Um, an appropriate motion would be to move Bill Number 1042 to the Committee of the Whole. Is there a mo

tion? Representative Frey. Thank you, Madam Chair. I move House Bill 26-1042 to the Committee of the Whole with a favorable recommendation. Second. Badly seconds. Okay, can we— okay, uh, Mr. Shadun, can you call the roll? Girl. Representative Barone. Yes. Bradfield. Oh, we didn't— yes. Representative Bradfield, I'm sorry, I missed that. Oh, that's right. Bradley. Yes. English. Pass. Bray. Yes. Hamrick. Yes. Johnson. Respectfully, yes. McCormick. Yes. Ryden. Yes. Stewart. Yes. Woog. Yes. Goldstei

n. Oh, excused. Who passed? Representative English? Yes, Madam Chair. And yes, with, uh, looking forward to seeing the amendments on seconds. Passes 12 to 0 with 1 excused. You're on your way to the Committee of the Whole. The Health and Human Services Committee is adjourned for today. Yikes, I broke it.

utterances.speaker: Rep. Hamrick
utterances.text: Network leasing, which is sometimes labeled rental networks or passive PPOs, allows an insurance company to lease a dentist's contracted rate to other insurance companies without the dentist's direct agreement. That means a dentist who signs a contract with one plan suddenly becomes an in-network provider for multiple plans that they have never reviewed, negotiated, or consented to.

utterances.speaker: Chair Gilchrist
utterances.text: Once this happens, it can be exceedingly difficult or near impossible for a provider to opt out of these plans. For patients, this leads to confusion and potential financial harm. Patients select a dentist believing they're seeing an in-network provider and schedule care based on that understanding.

utterances.speaker: Rep. Hamrick
utterances.text: Once the patient is seen for care, they may receive different coverage levels, unexpected limitations, higher out-of-pocket costs. This results in frustration, surprise bills, and a breakdown in trust with their healthcare provider. House Bill 1070 addresses these problems by increasing transparency and requiring consent and disclosure when networks are leased.

utterances.speaker: Chair Gilchrist
utterances.text: It ensures that if a dentist's contract is going to be extended to another carrier, it happens clearly, deliberately, with accountability, and with the knowledge of the provider.

utterances.speaker: Rep. Hamrick
utterances.text: So in essence, this is true transparency.

utterances.speaker: Chair Gilchrist
utterances.text: Networks that are expanded through leasing Insurance are able to advertise broad access without actually negotiating contracts with these providers.

utterances.speaker: Rep. Hamrick
utterances.text: It distorts the size of the provider market and ultimately reduces the true access to care for some providers as they limit participation or leave networks entirely because they can't operate under the undisclosed and not agreed-upon fee schedules. This instability can hurt patients, especially seniors, families on fixed incomes, and those in rural communities.

utterances.speaker: Chair Gilchrist

panel meetings. The board is divided into 3 panels: 1 licensing panel and 2 inquiry panels. xample, one inquiry panel currently contains 1 member of the public and 1 physician assistant, while the other inquiry panel currently has 2 members of of the public and no physician assistant. crimination, implicit or explicit bias, negligent clinical decision-making, denial of care, or other discriminatory or negligent misconduct— these issues may have contributed to the severe maternal morbidity or death. penalties against a healthcare practitioner who is found to have engaged in discriminatory or negligent misconduct that led to severe maternal morbidity or death.
